findings.title: The device count and the insert are separate steps, so requests that arrive together can go over the limit.
findings.body: `CountDevices` and the upsert after it are not in one transaction and take no lock. If several new devices authenticate at the same moment while the count is `limit-1`, they all see a count below the limit and all insert. The configured limit is then exceeded. Run the count and the insert in one transaction with suitable locking, or use a conditional insert, if the limit has to hold exactly.

findings.title: `args` gets the query prepended again each time `WithDbSession` retries the closure.
findings.body: `args = append([]interface{}{query}, args...)` changes the variable from the enclosing function inside the session callback. `WithDbSession` reruns the callback on retryable errors, such as SQLite `database is locked`. On a rerun, `args` already starts with the query, so the query is prepended a second time. `Exec` then gets the SQL string as a bind parameter and the wrong number of arguments, and the update fails. Build the slice in a local variable inside the closure, e.g. `execArgs := append([]interface{}{query}, args...)`.

findings.title: On MySQL, an existing device that is already within the limit can be refused because 0 rows were changed.
findings.body: By default, MySQL's `RowsAffected` counts only rows whose values actually change, not rows that match. If the limit is reached and an existing device sends a request with the same IP and user agent within the same second as its stored `updated_at` (MySQL stores seconds), the UPDATE matches the row but changes nothing. It returns 0, and the device gets `ErrDeviceLimitReached` and is locked out. Before returning the limit error, check whether the row exists, e.g. `SELECT 1 ... WHERE device_id=? AND updated_at BETWEEN ...`.

findings.title: A device that was refused can get in on its next request because the local cache still holds its tag.
findings.body: `TagDevice` → `tagDeviceUI` checks the local cache first. In the current implementation it also sets the cache key *before* it calls `CreateOrUpdateDevice`. When a new device hits the limit, the first request gets `ErrDeviceLimitReached` and is refused. The cache entry stays, though, so every request from the same device in the next ~29 minutes returns nil from `tagDeviceUI` and logs in anonymously. The limit only stops one request per device per cache period. I could not see `tagDeviceUI` itself. Fix: set the cache key only after `CreateOrUpdateDevice` succeeds, or delete it when the store returns an error.
